stops.name: San Isidro, Villa Miralrío, the convalescence begins
stops.campa: In the villa Victoria has rented and furnished for him at her own expense, Tagore recovers slowly under her daily supervision: she brings him fruit, sits with him through his fevers and lucid intervals, defends him from Buenos Aires society's eagerness to lionize a still-sick man. He begins in these weeks to write in Bengali again, poems that will not be published until his return to India; several he translates himself into English at her particular request, so that she, who reads no Bengali, can know at once what he is making of his exile on her river.

stops.name: San Isidro, the naming: Vijaya
stops.campa: As the weeks pass Tagore gives his hostess a Sanskrit name, Vijaya, meaning victory, a direct translation of her own; he will use no other name for her in the poems and letters of the rest of his life. Something passes between the two that neither calls simply friendship and neither calls simply love: a devotion at once filial, romantic, and reverent, conducted in a language of gesture and translated verse across a gulf of age, culture, and tongue neither can fully close. She keeps, afterward, the chair he sat in; visitors to her house will be shown it for fifty years.

stops.name: San Isidro, departure and the dedication of Purabi
stops.campa: After two months, recovered, Tagore sails on. Back in India he gathers the twenty poems written mostly at Villa Miralrío into a book he calls Purabi, an evening raga of Indian classical music, and dedicates the whole collection to Vijaya. It is the only book of his to carry a dedication to a person outside his own family and country. The two will meet only once more, in France in 1930; but the correspondence, and the name, outlast the single encounter by more than fifty years, running to Victoria's own old age.

stops.name: Madrid, De Francesca a Beatrice, the first book
stops.campa: Written first in French and rendered into Spanish by Ricardo Baeza, Victoria's confession of what Dante's Comedy meant to her is published in Madrid by Ortega y Gasset's own Revista de Occidente, with an epilogue by Ortega himself: her first book, at thirty-four, appearing under the imprint of the man who two years later will help her found her own. It is read as a daring, intimate act for a woman of her class, a public unveiling of private feeling through the armor of medieval poetry; the reviews notice both the theme and the fact that a rich Argentine lady has dared to write at all.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, meeting Jorge Luis Borges through Güiraldes
stops.campa: Through their shared friend Ricardo Güiraldes, the theosophist gaucho-novelist who will die of cancer three years later, Victoria meets the young Jorge Luis Borges, not yet the writer he will become. The friendship that begins here is lasting and difficult, marked by admiration on both sides and by Borges's later, famous, backhanded praise: that everything she has done seems to him remarkable, the magazine, the publishing house, the gathering of such notable people, as if the achievement were social rather than literary. He will nonetheless publish the bulk of his stories, poems, and essays first in the magazine she has not yet founded.
stops.quote: Todo lo que ella ha hecho me parece muy notable: la revista, la editorial, el hecho de haber reunido a gente tan notable.
stops.quote_source: Borges, quoted in La Nación, 'Borges y Victoria: la pasión de una amistad difícil'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the arrival of Count Keyserling
stops.campa: The German philosopher-count Hermann von Keyserling, already famous for his Travel Diary of a Philosopher, comes to lecture in Buenos Aires and is drawn at once into Victoria's intimate circle; he will describe afterward a relationship strangely intense and at the same time unreal, conducted half in the open and half concealed from a curious city. Out of the tour comes his book Meditaciones suramericanas, and out of the entanglement, twenty years later, her own reply, El viajero y una de sus sombras, published only after his memoirs draw her portrait in terms she does not accept as her own.

stops.name: Paris, Pierre Drieu la Rochelle falls in love
stops.campa: In Paris, after a lunch shared with Ortega y Gasset, the French writer Pierre Drieu la Rochelle confesses to his own wife that he has fallen in love with the Argentine visitor; a second meeting begins an affair conducted on long walks through the city, intense enough that some later say it is the cause of his separation from his wife Olésia. The correspondence between Victoria and Drieu will run, on and off, until his suicide in 1945 amid the ruin of his collaborationist politics, and will be published decades later as Lettres d'un amour défunt.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the first number of Sur
stops.campa: Urged for years by Ortega, Waldo Frank, and Eduardo Mallea, Victoria launches, at her own expense and under her own direction, the literary review Sur. The first issue, four thousand copies, sells out within weeks and is carried to Paris and Madrid as well. Its foreign council reads like a map of the century's letters, Ortega, Frank, Drieu, Ansermet, Alfonso Reyes; its Argentine board includes Borges, Mallea, Girondo, González Garaño. For the next four decades, through 372 numbers, it will be the single narrowest gate through which European and North American modernism enters Spanish America, and through which Argentina answers back.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Editorial Sur founded
stops.campa: Two years after the magazine, Victoria extends the enterprise into a publishing house, Editorial Sur, again financed from her own family fortune and again counseled by Ortega, Frank, and Mallea. Over the following decades the house will bring into Spanish, often for the first time and often in translations she has personally solicited or supervised, Virginia Woolf, Aldous Huxley, D. H. Lawrence, Graham Greene, Faulkner, and a long roll of others; the two enterprises together, review and house, make her for forty years the single most consequential literary broker between the Río de la Plata and the wider world.

stops.name: Buenos Aires, Drieu la Rochelle's Argentine tour
stops.campa: Invited by Sur, Pierre Drieu la Rochelle disembarks in Buenos Aires and is welcomed at once into Victoria's circle and into a solid friendship with Borges; encouraged by him she has Drieu taken on a tour of the Argentine interior, where he lectures on the crisis of European democracy to audiences that do not yet know he will end, thirteen years later, a collaborator with the German occupation and a suicide. The affair begun in Paris continues here, uneasily, in the full daylight of the city that knows her; it will not survive the coming decade of politics, though the letters between them do.

stops.name: London, meeting Virginia Woolf
stops.campa: At a photography exhibition by Man Ray, Victoria is introduced to Virginia Woolf; the two women will meet in person only three times in their lives, yet build between these rare meetings a correspondence at once literary and deeply personal. Victoria wins from her, in this same visit, the right to translate and publish A Room of One's Own in Spanish, and, in principle, To the Lighthouse and Orlando as well: the beginning of a project that will occupy Editorial Sur, and the household of Jorge Luis Borges's own mother, for the next several years.

stops.name: Rome, the interview with Mussolini
stops.campa: On a European trip Victoria secures and publishes an interview with Benito Mussolini, whom she first describes, to her own later shame, in terms close to admiration, calling him a kind of genius of order. The judgment does not survive the year: when Italy invades Abyssinia she appends a sharply critical note to the published interview, and within two years Sur declares itself openly and permanently against fascism, aligning the magazine with European liberalism and, as the Spanish Civil War opens, with the Republican cause against Franco.
